utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Now, today all the accused are present. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes, and that's it. Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes. Good afternoon to you, sir. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue and hopefully finish with your testimony today. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Neskovic. As the Presiding Judge has already told you, I will try and finish my examination-in-chief as soon as possible today. When we left it off yesterday, we were talking about the 11th of July. I would like to take you back to that time, as I say, where we left it off yesterday. With regard to the state, I would like to ask you whether you had any information about members of the PJP from the public security station in Bratunac with regard to their activities on that particular day, on the 11th of July. Were they engaged in any activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that same evening they were supposed to go on a field mission. However, at that particular time I was at home on furlough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But while you were at the police station, were you able to notice anything that would regard the activities of the members of the 1st company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from my station who belonged to that company had already been equipped to go on a field mission, as I've already told you, and one group - and I wouldn't be able tell you how many men I saw in that group - arrived in front of that station. They were talking to each other. I suppose they were discussing their joint field mission. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when your shift was over on the 11th of July, what did you do next? Did you go somewhere? If you did, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like any other day, I went straight to my apartment and I stayed there until the following morning when I returned to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now this brings us to the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's look at 4D620, page 24 in the B/C/S version or page 1 in the English version of that same text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's just wait for the relevant page to appear on e-court. Do you see the entry for the 12th of July? It says here that at that time you were at the public security station from 7.00 in the morning until 1700 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you really in the station all that time on the 12th of July? I'm talking about the time between 7.00 and 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there all the time. During the morning hours, or, to be more precise, around 10.00 in the morning, out of curiosity I went to Potocari. My intention was to look up two of my friends, and if I saw them I wanted to extend my assistance, if I could extend any. And that's where I stayed for about an hour. This was my only absence from the police station. The rest of the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us that curiosity took you to Bratunac. Let me ask you this: Did somebody ask you to go there? Did you ask any officers' approval or any of your superiors' approval?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ordered me to go there. I just informed the deputy commander, Branimir Tesic. He also wanted to join me because allegedly he had a relative there, and he wanted to see whether he would be able to locate him in that large group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a small correction in the transcript, page 3, line 21. It says here: "He also wanted to join me..." Brano Tesic wanted to join you. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you left the police station. According to your best recollection, it was around 10.00. You were together with Brano Tesic. Was anybody else with you on that occasion when you left the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the car. There were just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there in Potocari, what did you see there? What was the situation there like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an ugly scene for me. There were a few thousand people as if they were on a village fair. There were -- they were fenced off by plastic bands, and in front of the plastic bands there were members of the Serb military, soldiers, and also officers from the UNN.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And while you were there in Potocari, did you have an occasion to see Mr. Borovcanin at any point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us that you wanted to look up two of your friends and that Brano Tesic wanted to find a relative of his, if possible. Did that materialise? Did you see your friends? Did you find them, and did Brano Tesic find his relative?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see these people. I probably would have stayed longer, but many people knew me. They were calling my name. I couldn't bear that. I could not help everybody. I could not even maybe help the two that I was looking for. It would have been hard to do. It was war. So I returned, and Tesic stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. According to your best recollection, when was it when you returned to the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been no later than noon, 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And while you were in Potocari, did you have an occasion or an opportunity to see whether the Serb forces separated men from their families? Is that something that you were able to see in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that at the moment. Everybody was still. Everybody was where the army had put them, and the military was in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And were you able to see members of the Serb forces committing any acts of violence against the Muslim population gathered there in Potocari? Did you see anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And one more question with this regard. Did you perhaps have an occasion to see the arrival of a large number of buses and lorries in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, they didn't arrive. But on my way back from Potocari to Bratunac, which is a distance of about 5 kilometres, I came across some ten or dozen buses moving in that direction. I suppose that that was where they were headed for, but I can't be sure of that, but I did see them on the road headed in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You've already told us that you returned to the police station. On that same day, on the 12th of July, did the Bratunac police station send out any patrols?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, there were practically no stuff at the police station because many had left with the station commander to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's talk about something else. We'll come back to the Srebrenica event later. Do you remember whether there were any patrols at the disposal of the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most necessary services, the most indispensable services in town had to operate, so the town patrol was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And while answering my question, you said that on that day the public security station in Srebrenica was established. Let us look at a document with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P58.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, in the preparation for your testimony, you were shown this document. Do you have a good view of it in front of you? I can see you leaning closer to it. So this is an order issued on the 12th of July, 1995. In the heading, it says Republika Srpska, Ministry of the Interior, office of the minister. This was sent to the public security centre in Zvornik to the chief thereof. And if we look at page 1, we will see firstly that the deputy Minister of the Interior conveys the order issued by the President of the Republika Srpska issued on the 11th of July, 1995. And after that, if we look at the second page. Can we please move to the second page of the document. You can see here that pursuant to the order referred to on page 1 of this document, I hereby issue the following order: Under 1, "On the 12 of July, 1995, establish a public security station in Srebrenica." And then under 2: "Choose the senior staff of the SJB in accordance with the procedure laid down in the provisions of the law on internal affairs." I don't intend to go on reading the whole document, but now that you've had another look at it, could you tell me whether the timeframe corresponds to what you were telling us about the establishment of the public security station in Stanica? In other words, did this indeed happen on the date stated herein?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, Slavo Mladjenovic, the commander of the police station, went with a certain number of men to Srebrenica. That's as much as I know, and I know that that was their mission. And I know that Petko Pavlovic was ear-marked for the chief of the public security station in Srebrenica, and this is all I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you whether you perhaps know. You said that Slavoljub Mladjenovic had taken a certain number of men with him and had gone to Srebrenica to establish the police station. Do you know if the policemen that went with Slavoljub Mladjenovic, did they long to a PJP company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they belonged to 2nd company because this gentleman was the officer of the 2nd company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, on the 12th of July, when your shift was over, what did you do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as the day, before I went to my apartment where I was resting until the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you about your arrival in Potocari and whether you had an occasion to see Mr. Borovcanin there. And now let me ask you about the rest of the day, the 12th of July when you were no longer in Potocari. Did you see Mr. Borovcanin at any time during that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at exhibit 4D620, page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have already looked at that same page. Let's look the entry for the 13th of July. It says again that you were at the police station from 7.00 in the morning until 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 13th of July, do you remember that something happened, something that stayed imprinted in your memory that concerned a member of the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to work in the morning at 7.00, the deputy of the police station commander, Nedeljkovic, Dragan, told me that in the health centre there was a corpse that had been brought there and said I should go and see who it was. When I went to the health centre or to the clinic, I recognised my colleague, the late Ninkovic, Zeljko -- Zeljko Ninkovic. I returned to the police station. I informed my seniors of the fact, and I was then assigned the task that I should go to his family house, see his parents, and carry out the necessary preparations. In the case of the Serbs, this is a lengthy process. You have to prepare; you eat meat; you drink; it's like a wedding, but people are not in a happy mood. You have to have a meal at the late man's home. You have to have a wake until the following day when the funeral is held. Towards the end of my working day, I returned to the police station to see what else had to be done, and I remained until the end of my duty in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During that time, while you involved in these activities, did you have the opportunity of seeing a bus -- or buses passing through Bratunac and seeing where they were heading?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I did not -- or could not see any such thing. But I did see a bus in the evening on the previous day passing by my building because the Srebrenica-Zvornik road is there. So whenever a vehicle passes by, I can see that vehicle and hear it. This is something that either that you forgot to mention or I forget to mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that after those preparations, for the funeral of Zeljko Ninkovic you were very busy, but then at one point in time you returned to the Bratunac police station. Can you tell me whether there are any other events on the 13th on July that you could mention after you had returned to the police station? Were there any over events that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind, but the end of my working day, or perhaps I lingered on there for 10 or 15 minutes in the police station because I met a colleague who was arriving at work. He was one of my younger colleagues, and we spoke to each other in the corridor about how to carry everything out and how to secure a sufficient number of people who weren't engaged for the following day when the funeral was to be held. While I was speaking to my colleague, I heard rapid steps, and Mr. Borovcanin entered. I was somewhat surprised by his behaviour because I know that he is a calm man. He entered in a quite rapid manner, and if I remember this correctly, he said, Niko, what's going on? What's being done? Give me a phone quickly. I have to phone the brigade. I just had a look at him. I couldn't say a word. My colleague and I said, well, you know that the communications centre is further up, and he passed by. He went on, went up to the floor to the room where there were communications. And then I returned home, and I didn't leave until the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you have just said that another colleague of yours was present at the scene. Could you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavisa Simic, and I assume that Branimir Tesic was also in the office, although, I didn't open the door. I saw the door was closed, but I don't think he had locked the door, so I assumed that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin wanted to contact the brigade. Did you find out whether he managed to contact them? Did you hear anything about what Mr. Borovcanin had to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the ground floor, and the communications centre was up on another floor across the -- opposite the office of Mr. Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. A general question now. We are dealing with July 1995. It's not in dispute that Mr. Borovcanin was the deputy commander of the special police brigade at the time, and you have also told us about the duties that you had to perform. In the light of -- in the line of command, could Mr. Borovcanin issue orders to you or to someone else in the Bratunac police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Borovcanin, for example, asked for assistance of some kind, for example, if he wanted to phone from the premises or to send a telegram or something like that, would you have done that for him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. Assistance is one thing. An order is another thing. We would have probably helped him if that is what was at stake, but it would have had to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from what you have just told us with regard to that meeting with Mr. Borovcanin in the police station in Bratunac on the 13th of July, so apart from what you have just told us, is there anything else that you can remember about that meeting that you would like to mention?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have nothing further to add with regard to the meeting. It was very brief, and there was nothing much said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And after this event, as you have already said you left the premises of the police station. Could you tell us where you went?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to my flat, and I remained there until the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's now have a look at the exhibit that we have had a look at on a number of occasions, 4D620, and that's the same page, page 24. I'd like to have a look at the entry for the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We can see that on the 14th of July you have an entry that concerns the period from 7 to 1700 hours in the police station. Tell me, on the 14th of July, during this period referred to here, the ten hours, did you remain in the police station in Bratunac or did you go outside, and if so, where did you go and when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't spend much time in the police station on that day. When I arrived in the morning, I checked everything, did what was necessary, and then I started organising the funeral of the late Ninkovic. I remained there then until the very end of my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you went to the funeral of the late Ninkovic on that day. Apart from yourself, do you remember whether there were any other staff members of Bratunac police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was some people, so to speak, at hand from the 1st company. They didn't go out into the field. They were gathered or assembled to perform a ceremonial shooting, and then there were some others who were assembled to carry out the funeral itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to ask you about several other events that have to do -- or that transpired on the 13th and 14th of July. Can you tell me whether you have any information according to which on the 14th of July some of the senior police station members went to Bratunac? Did you hear anything about this? Did you see any such individuals? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that my duty was over in the police station and that I was going home, I heard that Mr. Kovac had been present - I don't know whether he had been in the police station - but I had heard that he'd -- or that he was going to Srebrenica. That's what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see him, and I told you that I was at the funeral until the end of my working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have a few more questions I would like to put to you with regard to these dates. Can you tell me whether you heard anything about events in the Kravica agricultural cooperative on the 13th of July, 1995? Did you hear anything about such events? If so, when? From whom? What did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't tell you from whom I heard about this because the rumor spread after the funeral when we had this lunch. Those who were present spoke to each other, and they said that in Kravica -- or, rather, a group of Muslims or Bosniaks had surrendered in Kravica, and they were being detained in buildings that belonged to the Oka, to this agricultural association. They then tried to break out of the building, apparently. They killed a policeman, took his rifle. They wounded another policeman, and on that occasion there was a clash. A fight broke out, and a certain number of Muslims were killed. That's what I heard. Those are the stories that I heard, but I never went there. A month or two after the event, I didn't go there. It wasn't necessary, so there was nothing for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was the event in Kravica discussed in Bratunac? Was it a subject that was discussed in public and frequently?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. As soon as two individuals meet, they will talk about irregular events. So -- and that was included in the stories told. There was the version that I heard and that I have told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apart from what you have just told us, is there anything else you know about these events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's nothing more precise that I could add. If I knew anything else, I'd tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would now like to ask you something about another subject, and it relates to the same dates. Did you at any point in time hear that on the 13th, at night, in 1995 a certain number of detained Muslims or captured Muslims arrived in Bratunac and they were put up in the Vuk Karadzic school. They spent the night in Bratunac. Did you hear anything about this, or did you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. Whatever happens at night -- well, at the time I wasn't really working at night. It wasn't necessary for me to be in the building where I work, either. So I can hear stories from others, and then I can speculate about such events. I did hear that there was a certain number of buses that stopped there. They went on towards Zvornik and Kladanj in the morning, but I personally did not witness this, and my colleagues who were on duty in town don't submit reports to me but to their superiors. And sometimes these stories weren't stories that would come to me. I was excluded from these stories because, you know, when certain generations change, when young people arrive -- well, if you're a communist policeman, a policeman from Tito's regime, then it's more difficult for you to have access to such information through stories that circulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the knowledge you have is based on what others have told you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you have spoken about your movements. We've analysed this. We've analysed the events of the 14th of July, and after all these events what happened in the course of your duties? Did anything in particular happen after the 14th of July that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's funny to say this, perhaps, but the following days passed by quite normally as if nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you met Mr. Borovcanin in the police station. You've testified about this already, and at some subsequent point in time in the course of July, did you perhaps have the opportunity of seeing him again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can claim that I -- with certainty that I didn't see the gentleman again that year. When he left the brigade, he went to the police administration. I think on one occasion he then came to the police station, and I think that I saw him then, but apart from that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now I have just a few questions for you. The name Miroslav Stanojevic, does it ring any bells with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are hinting at the same man, there are many men bearing that same name, but there was a younger man called Miroslav, a member of the Red Berets. I believe that he was killed a few years ago an in a traffic accident, if that's the person you're referring to. I don't know any other person by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And finally let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, just to give you an indication. You remember yesterday we spoke of having shorter sessions and shorter breaks just to give the opportunity to the witness to rest his back?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will certainly do this. I believe that I have, like, five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Because I was suggesting that we have the break at 15.15, at quarter past 3, for 15 minutes and then resume. So as soon as you finish, we can have the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we can, rather, have a break now, and then I will be -- just to make sure that I cover everything that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 15-minute break now. --- Break taken at 3.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Neskovic, I have just a couple of questions left for you, and this will bring my examination-in-chief to an end. Could you please tell me, when were you first contacted by the Borovcanin Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the summer of this year. I believe it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And after that initial contact, did you have any other contacts with the Defence team before your arrival here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in September, also this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you've mentioned July and September, and before you arrived here in The Hague, did you have any other contacts with the Defence team? I'm not referring to the victims and witnesses unit. I'm referring to any other contacts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no other contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neskovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is John Ostojic, and I represent Ljubisa Beara. How are you? Sir, I have on couple of questions that maybe you could help me with being a citizen of Bratunac in 1995 at the very least and before that. Can you tell me who Ljubisav Simic is or was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisav Simic was the president of the municipality for a time. I wouldn't be able to tell you for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in July of 1995 whether you saw him in or around Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was in Bratunac because he resided in the suburbs in his family house. He was there. I saw him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what date? Do you remember from some of the dates that you remember? I'm not sure if you could be more specific for us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were in Potocari and you went there for an hour, hour and a half or so. Do you remember if you saw Mr. Simic there at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What role, if any, did Mr. Simic play with the police station that you were at in Bratunac? Was he involved in it at all, or was he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not involved in the work of the police station. He couldn't. But while he was the president of the municipality [as interpreted], he may have had contacts with my superiors, with the commanders. And if there had been any such contacts, I can't tell you what their nature was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the transcript. I hate to interrupt, but the witness said while he was the president of the municipal assembly. That's what I heard from the witness and here it says "municipality" on page 18, line 8 -- or it's line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It will be corrected in due course. Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, for example, one of the superiors you're referring to is Mr. Miodrag Josipovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what I need to know from you if you remember, do you know if Dragomir Vasic was in Bratunac in July 1995 to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the dates that we were talking about, Dragomir Vasic was in Bratunac. His -- he shared his office with Josipovic, or Josipovic gave him the use of his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember in July of 1995 when it was that Dragomir Vasic first began sharing an office with Mr. Josipovic and when that ended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mention any dates, maybe the 9th or the 10th. I know that the staff was in Zvornik. They were monitoring the political situation there, and around the time of the events in Srebrenica they moved to my police station. But I can't tell you when they moved in and when they moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. A couple of follow-up questions on your answer. When you say "staff," you're referring to the Zvornik police staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you give us any idea if it was for more than two days or any estimate as to how many days this Zvornik police staff was stationed in the Bratunac police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can tell you is that it would be a minimum of three and a maximum of five days during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We mentioned some of the prominent political figures in Bratunac both in your direct and I think in your cross of Mr. Deronjic and Mr. Simic. What about Mr. Davidovic? Are you familiar with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During these events, Davidovic did not have a political role to play in any structure. He went to the lines like any other foot soldier. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to this police staff in Zvornik that was in Bratunac in July of 1995, what was the role of Dragomir Vasic at that time in connection with the Bratunac police station? Do you know what his duties and obligations were at that time? I know you mentioned to look at the political situation, but can you be more concrete for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a -- the superior to all of us, to my commander, to my chief, and to all the other officers in position who participated on that. I did not have any direct contacts with him. He never issued any orders to me directly, so I can't give you anything in any more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you ever shown or given documents that purportedly were signed by Dragomir Vasic during that time-period, the 12th, 13th, and 14th of July, 1995, to review? Have you ever seen any such orders or directives from Mr. Vasic at any time up to today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I have given you my job description, and that did not involve any contacts with them. The only orders I received from any of the officers, that was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a citizen of Bratunac called Dragan Mirkovic? Do you know who he is, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic. One moment, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise again, but I notice that there is the name of a person missing from the answer. It's page 20, line 13. "That was my immediate superior ..." I believe that the witness mentioned the name of this person, and I cannot see this in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who was your immediate superior, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slavoljub Mladjenovic was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know Dragan Mirkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how long have you known Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that his nickname? Ljubisav's nickname is Ljubo? I thought so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known him a somewhat shorter time. We not any contacts until towards the end of my police career. He was a school teacher, so I only knew him by sight, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the relationship was between Mr. Simic and Mr. Mirkovic, if any? Was it a close relationship? Were they mere acquaintances, or were they distant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. The place where we reside is small. We see each other often, but I never saw the two of them together. I did not see them socialize. As of recently, I've been socialising with Mirkovic somewhat more often, but I have not seen the two of them socialising. Maybe they have some business contacts. Mirkovic was the general manager of the utilities company. Maybe they have had some contacts because of that, but I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me turn a different topic, sir, given your experience in the Bratunac police station and how those structures work. I just wanted to clarify a couple of things, and you can help me here, and I'd appreciate that very much. The head of the police is actually the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... chief of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question. Even I had problem in understanding it. "The head of the police is actually the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, correct?" What does this mean? I really didn't understand. The translation was --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to make it so it's clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I understand it, but anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- if you could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. We'll just do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise if it was inartful, sir. Now, we have something called MUP, and you know what that is, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and in 1995 that existed, and at that time, either the minister or the deputy minister of the MUP in Republika Srpska was Tomo Kovac, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mention him, so I'm sure you know of him. Immediately below the structure of the MUP, you have what we've called and identified CJB, which is an acronym for centar -- Centar Javne Bezbednosti or centre, public security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And how many were there in the area of Bratunac and Zvornik that were known as CJBs? Was there only one, or were there more than one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I don't know if you were following, also, in the transcript, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the interpreters are complaining and try to write -- or the stenographers are complaining because you're going to fast. So if you could kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, and I apologise for going fast, but I just kind of want to get this, and there's really actually five levels to it, I think -- five levels, but we'll go through it slowly. We discussed MUP with Tomo Kovac. The next level immediately under that is the CJB, which is that Centar Javne Bezbednosti, or in English, the way we say it, the centre for public security. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many centres for public security were there in that area that we would call from Zvornik all the way through to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we draw a pyramid, there is the MUP at the very top. Below it are centres, and below them there are public security stations. In my part of the state in the Drina region, there was the Zvornik station with subordinated stations in Skelani, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Milici, Vlasenica, Osmaci, and Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you're getting ahead of me, and I agree with you there. Those separate sections that you've just identified, Skelani, Bratunac, Vlasenica, those were called Posebna Jedinica Policije or PJP, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SJB, public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was above the SJB, then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik centre, the centre in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In July of 1995, the chief guy, the number one guy of the centre in Zvornik was Dragomir Vasic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you mention those six or two other stations, public security stations that you had identified. Where does the PJP fall under? Is it below each one of those stations? Where is it in the hierarchy or the pyramid that you mentioned? Where does it fall under?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A PJP is part of the centre, but the commander of the centre orders each station to allocate a proportionate number of its men who would belong to the 1st company with the most capable youngest men, then the 2nd company consisting of lesser capable men, and so on and so forth. In any case, every PJP is subordinated to the centre. No CJB [as interpreted] could on its own incorporate or have on its strength a PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Now, you told us that Dragomir Vasic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Again, I have to correct the transcript. It does says here on page 24, line 13, "No CJB could on its own incorporate or have on its strength a PJP." He was referring to SJB, public station not centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if -- you told us about Tomo Kovac being in Bratunac in July sometime about the 14th, as best as you recall, and also Dragomir Vasic setting up basically his offices next to the commander Josipovic. Also, for a few days or so in July of 1995, just help me with this: Prior to that time in July of 1995, had there been any other instance where Dragomir Vasic or another chief of the - and I just want to get the right acronym here - CJB ever came to Bratunac to either perform any duties or obligations for an overnight stay?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not see that. There is a line along which the chief of the centre can invite or order any of his subordinated commanders to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It seems we have a constant problem with interpretation because there is -- I notice just a moment ago that here, what my colleague said was "CJB came to Bratunac." It's on page 25, line 8. But what was translated to the witness was SJB, so there is a lot of confusion here. So maybe I can just draw the attention to the interpreters and also to my colleague to be careful about his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Lazarevic. It's not your fault, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And really, I don't think it's that -- we're just trying to get --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we know Dragomir Vasic, the position he held. Let's not mention the position, but he held a certain position in July of 1995. He was in Bratunac at that time. What I am asking you, that Dragomir Vasic - and you may not know how long he held that function - but a few years prior to that or at any time to the best of your recollection, did Dragomir Vasic as a member of the Centar Javne Bezbednosti or anyone in his position as the chief of that organisation, did they ever come to Bratunac for an overnight stay to perform any functions and obligations, to the best of your recollection? And I know what you said theoretically, but I want to know factually. Do you remember anyone like that coming to Bratunac prior to July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any such instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me with this. I thought your testimony, and I'll share with you just generally - I think I'm right - that other people have testified that most of the police officers were not in Bratunac during the night of the 12th through the 14th or thereabouts, and I'm just generalising it here. If they were all gone, what was Dragomir Vasic doing there? Who was he actually giving orders to, or who was he directing or providing any supervision to? What was his role if all his men and the men below him were out on the field or on the terrain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. These questions should be put to people outside of my station. Dragomir Vasic had a circle of men who were subordinated to him with whom he worked. What they did, how they assigned their tasks, I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, do you know the names of any of these men who were in the circle of men who were subordinated to Vasic? Do you know any of their names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to my superiors from my station, I wouldn't know anybody else because I never had any contacts with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just a couple questions with respect to -- although I know you didn't see it yourself, but you heard that there were Bosnian Muslims who were held prisoner in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac, correct? Do you know anything about that or ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just share with you stories, speculations that I heard, but I don't want to speculate myself. If I've seen something, I would share that with you. And despite all of my health problems that I am suffering at the moment, if I had suffered like that at the time, I would have opposed that. I did not see. I heard that there were people detained there, but I can't tell you how many. I can't even tell you who I heard the story from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I am not suggesting otherwise, sir, and I respect that, and thank you for sharing with me. What I want to know is, did the entire town know? Did people like in these -- what we call powerful positions, like Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Simic, Mr. Davidovic, would they also have known or heard if they were in town that there were Bosnian Muslims being held in the Vuk Karadzic school to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's your comment to that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No comment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed with your next question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you learn what action, if any, the political authorities took in connection with either the buses that were at Bratunac or the Bosnian Muslim men who were held prisoner in the Vuk Karadzic school? Do you know what role, if any, they played in trying to either to move them or in trying to provide anything to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, higher politics are far from me, distant from me. What their intentions were, I don't know. What they were thinking, I don't know. These people were supposed to be moved to Zvornik, Tuzla, and Kladanj, I believe, and allegedly they were put up there just to refresh -- freshen up and to be given water to drink and move on. That's what I heard, but I can't tell you anything about the whole situation from what I know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, for helping.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any way in searching your memory you can tell us who it was that told you that all those men that were spending the night in Bratunac on the 13th, all those Muslims were there to freshen up and then to be moved on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago that I had heard stories in town, but I can't give you any names because I can't remember anybody in specific. There is no name attached to any of these stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you went to Potocari and observed there, did you know -- had you heard of the name of Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the name, but I never saw the man. I never had any contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you described someone as a communist police officer from the Tito days. Were you referring to yourself when you said that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you change your political viewpoint at some point and become a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always in favour of acting professionally. I was least interested in the grouping I would belong to. I acted in accordance with the rules. I wasn't in favour of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, were you ever a member of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in July of 1998, the Office of the Prosecutor searched the SDS offices of Miroslav Deronjic, and I want to show you a -- I am going to show you the originals so you can maybe tell us about it a bit. You've already told us the village you were from. Can you remind us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That should be 65 ter 3852.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the village you were born in? Pobrdje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pobrdje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that near Potocac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Potocac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know Mirko Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Jovo Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nikola Obrevic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you go to the third page. It's page 3 in the English. It should be page 3 of the -- it may -- yes, page 3 of the B/C/S, and --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This says "Local board." What local board is that? I mean, is that you, Neskovic Dragan, or is there another Neskovic Dragan in that village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time referred to here or the time that you referred to in 1998, I was living in my flat in Bratunac; and in village of Pobrdje there was a Dragan Neskovic, son of the late Radisa Neskovic who died two years ago. He, too, died two years ago. At the time, I didn't live in Pobrdje, so if there's anything else you were interested in, try and find out about it, I didn't join up. But as far as Obrevic Nikola is concerned, well, his ideas always bothered me. I came across them in various stories. So this document isn't evidence for me, but if it is evidence, well, it has to do with Dragan Neskovic, son of Radisa, whose mother is named Stana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I wasn't asking you about 1998. I was just telling you that's when the material was picked up. But I was asking about the wartime period. Were you ever a member of the SDS in the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never even crossed my mind at the time, and that's also the case now, and that will be the case for the future. It never crossed my mind to be a member of any party, and in particular, of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that other Dragan Neskovic a member of the wartime SDS from your village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. This was a young person with whom I did not have any contacts. I couldn't be certain about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that Dragan Neskovic's father's name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Radisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what year was that other Dragan Neskovic born?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either in 1960 or in 1961, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you aware in 1992 -- were you a police officer in 1992 in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have mentioned that you think Mr. Borovcanin came over in maybe July or August of 1992 to take the job of komandir of the police, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was in the summer in July/August. I don't know which month exactly, but roughly speaking, that was the period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at 65 ter number 3850.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You should get a B/C/S -- or a Serbian version of this up on your screen, but I'll -- to save a little time, it says "SJB Bratunac," and it says: "The list of active employees who carried out tasks and duties of the public security station during the month of July 1992," and "to whom the advanced money of salary has been paid for this month." Have you ever seen a document like this before? It looks like there are signatures to the right-hand side, and unless that's the other Dragan Neskovic, take a look at number. Maybe they'll blow it up a bit for you. Do you remember a document like this? It just says that -- it lists the police officers and the salary.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that look genuine to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so by this document, it would indicate Ljubomir Borovcanin, commander, was working there as well. Does that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, staying in 1992 just for a minute, do you recall a point where many Muslim civilians, both women and children and men, were detained in the Bratunac stadium and the men were separated from the women and put in the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. This is out of the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what's your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They've, you know, established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's always safe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- comment? All right. Mr. Neskovic, can you kindly remove your headphones; and before you do so, do you speak English? If he can put them back. Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not a single word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not even yes or no? Remove your headphones, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't intend to get into this topic at length, obviously. We have heard references to this historic event repeatedly over the couple of years. Basically, I want to ask him for credibility purposes. We have been talking a bit about 92 throughout. The witness Ljubisav Simic, there is quite a bit of evidence about the Vuk Karadzic school in evidence now from his 92 ter statement that went in. I chose not to talk to him about it, though I could have, to save a little bit for this witness. Not much, just a couple of questions related to it. And it will be based on evidence I do have. This is not a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours -- if I can ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. What Mr. McCloskey says when he says "basically," is this for the credibility purpose or not? So just to be clear about this, because if it's related to credibility about this witness, then it's okay, but if there is some other purpose, then I will -- it's a standing objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand basically it means that that is the main aim or purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. And in addition, Mr. President, you may recall the witness's answers that he went Potocari to see friends, to look up friends, as if, you know, old friends are going to be willing, you know, to hug each other and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We have already taken our decision, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Lazarevic. You are authorised to proceed with the question and any follow-ups, but please do it as brief and expeditious a manner as possible, and try to move to something different as early as possible too. Okay. Thank you for your patience, Mr. Neskovic. I would suggest you repeat the question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, were you working in Bratunac, and do you recall the event in May of 1992 when a large number of Muslim population, women and men, were taken to the Bratunac stadium and able-bodied men were separated and put in the Vuk Karadzic school and the women and children were transported out? Do you know of that occurrence or something resembling that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I could see. As you know, I said that in the course of my work in and out -- in and outside of the police station, I didn't have any other duties apart from when I had to go out for some --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt. I think you're in 1995. I'm taking you back to May 1992, the beginning of the war period, the first conflicts, okay? So -- and then my question was -- we don't need a big description of this event. We just want to know if -- do you recall the event or something like what I had described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started telling you what I knew about. It's a fact that people were assembled at the stadium, but it was a group that had turned up out of the blue. There were some volunteers. It was over a period of a few days, and then they just disappeared. Who they were, where they went, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're referring to the Muslim population that appeared out of the blue and then disappeared, or the volunteers from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He never said Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He's quoting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're right. He didn't. So what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Mr. Neskovic, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have partially answered the question. I said that some kind of a group of volunteers appeared. I didn't know any of them. I had never heard about them. I had never seen them. They assembled there. There was this looting, and they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about the Muslim population from the villages surrounding Bratunac. Are you aware that they were assembled in the stadium in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the answer that the witness gave - I apologise to my colleague - he said, "They assembled the population." That's what the witness said. They assembled people there. That's what was said on page 35, line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, these Muslim people that were assembled, were they separated as I've described, with the men being sent to Vuk Karadzic school, the women being shipped away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that because I wasn't there to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you're a trained police officer. I am sure you were, you know, aware of this situation. Can you just tell this Court if that happened, to the best of your knowledge, that the men were separated and put in the Vuk Karadzic school and the women were shipped out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know what you want me to do. This is not my job. I told you where I worked. I told you what I did. I couldn't see what was happening. And these speculations as to what someone said and so on and so forth, well, I don't want to go into that because I can't testify about the truth in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you saying you know nothing about the movement of the able-bodied men from the stadium to the Vuk Karadzic school back in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know nothing, but what kind of evidence would it be if I tell you about something I heard that happened three days ago, and then I'm told about it, and then I tell you about that? I won't accept something like that. It wouldn't be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, I have a statement from a Muslim from that school that said you were there at the school with those Muslims; is that correct? In May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave 1992 behind. These PJP units, these combat units that went to assist in combat that were part of the CSB Zvornik, can you tell us when police officers were first organised in units like the PJP units of 1995 and sent out for combat missions? Let's forget 1992. How about 1993? Were there police officers in Bratunac that got assembled as part of the combat units to go help the army or go take part in combat in other areas outside of their normal police duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to remember all the details. Sometimes the line would be attacked, the population would be a threat, and the policemen who were able to assist would go to the line to defend the line. But as to whether there was an organised unit from the police station in Bratunac that went out into the field on an independent basis, no, no such thing existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you know it existed in July of 1995 because you've talked to us specifically about it. Do you remember when that kind of organised assistance first happened? Was it 1995, 1994? I'm not asking for details. This is just pretty basic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think the unit was formed in 1994, perhaps in the second half of that year. I am not sure. I know that it was in existence in 1995 for sure, but I can't be certain when it comes to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've said that Mr. Borovcanin referred to you as Niko. What was Mr. Borovcanin's nickname?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I -- maybe I wasn't following that well, but I never heard the witness saying that Mr. Borovcanin referred to him by this nickname. I could be wrong, of course, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, he has accepted that proposition in any case. So why don't you move ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I don't see this. He didn't give his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe it's a translation issue, but what I heard over the translator was that when Mr. Borovcanin came in, he said something like "Niko, I need to use the phone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, he's in a position to answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you -- what did -- he didn't say that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use that term. I didn't have any nicknames at any time, and I never use nicknames for others. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not talk about nicknames, then. Let's talk about radio code names. What was the radio code name for this Bratunac SJB in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I didn't use the communications systems much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it would be convenient for you, Mr. McCloskey, it's one hour since we started this session. We need to have the 15 minute break we had agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have much more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will take a break of 15 minutes, and then we'll let him rest his back and everything. --- Break taken at 4.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you've explained to us that you were the logistics man for the police station. So can you tell us on those days - July 11th, 12th, 13th - where the police cars -- well, how many police cars did the Bratunac police station have, that period in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four or five cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And any trucks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had a four-wheel drive --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the end of your reply, Mr. Neskovic, if you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a four-wheel vehicle. All the other vehicles were passenger vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what kind of passenger vehicles, model?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volkswagens, Volkswagen Golfs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were they painted in a police colour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two of them were. The other two weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the colour of the ones that were painted in a police colour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that were painted, white and blue was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did they have any lights on them, obvious lights that were there on the top, I mean, not headlights. I figure they had headlights.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one of the vehicles had a rotational light; the others didn't. One was blue. The others were of a basic colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The non-blue and white cars, what were they -- what did they look like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was dark red, and the other was dark blue. Indigo is what we call that colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know what vehicle Mr. Borovcanin was using when he was in Bratunac on those days in July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say because when he came to the police station, when he was seen there, I don't know what kind of a vehicle he used. I didn't leave the building to be able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did your police vehicles get their fuel?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuel, oil, and other material would be obtained from a centre in Zvornik. I'd write down what we needed; I'd forward it to them; they'd secure the material; I'd go and pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So where did Bratunac police cars fill up their tanks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought fuel in metal barrels from Zvornik. Usually, I would load two or three 200-litre barrels. I would then unload them and store them in the storage, and then I would fuel from the barrels first using a hose, and then I got a pump from which I would then re-tank into buckets, and there I would refuel the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you the one who was personally responsible for re-fuelling police cars during this period, July 11th, 12th, 13 July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the police -- did your Golf police vehicles use more fuels on those days, the days that the Muslim population was being shipped out of the area, than they did normally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a strict rule on mileage. The vehicles could not make as many kilometres as people wanted, and by having inspected the fuel consumed, I could tell that the mileage that was done on those days was average.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did any Bratunac police cars follow or lead or escort in any way the buses full of Muslims that went from Potocari through Bratunac, passed Vlasenica, Tisca, dropping people off at Luka? Any police -- any Bratunac police cars take part in that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember. Not during those days. If somebody ever went - and I'm saying "if" - then it would be my officer who would have to know that. I would not have to know. I would just have to inspect the fuel, how much of it is left. I'm not the one who had an insight into the travel orders of the people using the vehicles. That's something that my officer, my superior officer would be privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there blue and white Golfs from other police departments that came to the Bratunac area during those days, the two days that the Muslims were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not excluding that possibility, but nobody ever turned to me to ask for any of the supplies from my storage. There were no such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we can see police cars escorting buses out of Potocari on a video. I take it you don't know a thing about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to my statement that I have repeated several times already. I worked in an office, in an enclosed building, from -- in no windows or doors could I see the streets. I could only see one square in my town. I could not see the transit of any of the vehicles. That view was blocked from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did any of those four police cars have radios in them, and I mean two-way radios?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me. The radios in the car were -- I can't really remember the make of those radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you would have been the one to resupply the broken antenna when that gets bent or the parts if somebody pulls off a microphone or kicks it or make sure it gets sent out for repair, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe you can describe the radios. I take it we're not talking about little handheld radios. We're talking about something attached to the car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you are asking me, but I really can't remember the make. I don't know whether it was a Motorola or a -- something of Czech production. It was a small set. It could almost fit in the pocket. It was indeed fixed, but I really don't know how else to describe that device because I can't remember the brand name or the make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, could a person -- a police officer with a radio like that in their car communicate to the Bratunac headquarters, say, from downtown Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not easy at the time because there were not enough repeaters, so you had to look for a suitable point in order to establish a connection across certain routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know Dragomir Stupar, the logistics guy from Sekovici, special police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
