utterances.text: We interviewed a person by that name that said he was the logistics officer and that he obtained material from Bratunac at a little warehouse on the main road to Srebrenica or a little building. Do you know what he's talking about? Surely, you must have worked with the police forces to help them stay supplied.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something new to me. It is the first time I hear that there are some other storages or depots. I was the only one. If there had been something else, I should have had to communicate with them and cooperate with them. I can vouch that this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps he was getting material from you, but you have no recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it's very hard to believe that I would issue something to somebody without knowing them. If I'd known him, I would have resupplied him, but I never heard the name before. The first time I hear the name is now, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to this time where you say Mr. Borovcanin came by the police department and asked to use the phone. Was that on the first day that Muslims were in Potocari or the second day they were in Potocari or another day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many days the Muslims stayed in Potocari. I am saying that the contact happened after my departure from Potocari. Whether they all left or not, I don't know. I can't say for sure. So on the day when I was in Potocari, the following day in the afternoon I saw Borovcanin and -- at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you go to Potocari the first day that Serb troops were in Potocari, or was it the second or third day that Serb troops were in Potocari, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I was in Potocari on the 12th of July before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you do remember the dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's unfair. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, let him answer the question. It's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you do remember the dates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a paper in front of me, and I saw it right there in front of me. The questions were put to me in a sequence following the course of the events as they unfolded, and that's how I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were taking your dates off the paper that was in front of you when you testified?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my memory still serves me. I may not be able to remember all the details. I may not be able to tie them to certain dates or days, but I certainly do remember those three or four days. I remember them well. They were well imprinted in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you told us you were looking at a piece of paper and the dates were on the paper. What were you looking at? You pointed at the screen, the TV screen. There is nothing wrong with refreshing your recollection from the TV screen or the paper. I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown those lists with the entries showing when I worked on those days. That's what I was referring to. I was shown those lists with my schedule during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it's possible you went to Potocari and saw the events the second day that Muslims were there, the second -- excuse me, the second day that Serb soldiers had gone to Potocari, and so that it was actually the following day that Mr. Borovcanin came by the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated. I stated that on the day before I saw Borovcanin, I'd gone to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you saw Mr. Borovcanin, did he tell you that one of his men had just been killed and one of his men had been injured, and he was just over at the health centre with the injured guy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not exchange any stories. On that second occasion, we never even shake -- shook hands. I've told you that his appearance at the police station was very sudden, very abrupt. He zoomed past me. He didn't even have time to shake hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At that time that you saw him, had you heard the reports of the Muslims, the dead Muslims at the Kravica warehouse, dead and dying Muslims, any report like that before Mr. Borovcanin zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said previously that the first time I heard about that was when we buried my late colleague, Zeljko Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neskovic, we have come to the end of your testimony. Our staff will give you all the assistance you need for your repatriation. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I will always remember your kindness and how good you were to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do have two documents. One is 4D620, and the other one is 4D621. The first one is CJB Bratunac attendance roster, and the other one is payroll for June 1992 from Kladanj police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the other Defence teams? None? So these documents are admitted. Mr. Ostojic, you don't have any documents. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. 65 ter number 3850, that list of active employees for July; and 3852, the list of the SDS members. I would also like to offer the July -- excuse me, the January and February SDS minutes indicating Mr. Borovcanin was a member -- or was recommended as a member and then a member of the SDS, as well, in response to his comment about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the third one -- for the first two, I have no objection. For the third one, first of all, this document was not used through this witness, and this is under objection. I believe Mr. Gosnell can explain that. He already filed an objection to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is a pending motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the reference number of this document? Is it 210 or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One of them is 210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the huge one, and all we wanted was I think January and February from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the -- I offer it because they offered evidence that, you know, he was not a member, if I remember correctly. So I would offer them again. I mean, it doesn't matter if something is involved in some sort of litigation. If it's -- if they're going to make an issue out of it again, I can bring in the material again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You have been called into cause, Mr. Gosnell, by your colleague. Do you wish to comment? It's obviously part of P210, which was objected to in your motion that I referred to yesterday. But it's only part of that, and it is relative to what Mr. McCloskey has just referred to. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, clearly there might be different issues in respect of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- different excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So I can't say for sure now having not looked at it if the same issues are in play or not. Well, if it -- but I do understand that it is the same excerpt, and accordingly, even if it's used in a different way with a different witness, we would take the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you will agree with me that even if P210 as objected to in your motion were to be excluded from testimony on the basis of the submissions contained in that motion, it doesn't necessarily follow that parts of it cannot be introduced today on a different basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's certainly true, Mr. President, but I think the more fundamental point here is the questions were asked; the witness answered; everything that is necessary for you to assess the witness's credibility is on the record; it's on the transcript; so we continue to objection to the admission of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- of this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly. I did not specifically ask this man about that particular document because he said he wasn't a member of the SDS and he had a name of another guy that was. And so I didn't want to take the time to show him a document that he clearly would have said "I've never seen before" or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I think I can bring in something else and offer it to -- as a credibility and impeachment issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, now I object more strongly because the document wasn't put to the witness to get a reaction. Now what's happening is that the document is actually being put in opposition to what the witness said, and that's highly improper. Now it is being used as evidence, so we do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the point of tendering P3852, which the witness denied being himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're going to do a little research on that one, Mr. President -- Your Honour, excuse me, to see if there are in fact two folks like that, and this is my only chance to offer it in, and it may be very relevant to his credibility. I don't take this man on his word on that. I just don't know. But I think given it was part of the questioning of the witness, part of the questioning of Mr. Ostojic earlier, apparently it was at 27412 that this was done. But it may become relevant. This is an issue, you know, who's a member and who's not of the SDS. It's something that was started, frankly, by the Defence. It's been moved on by the Borovcanin Defence, and it's something I want to be prepared for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- as it comes up next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Finished. I don't think we need to hear anymore submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Our decision is as follows: All the documents that you wish to tender or have asked to tender, Mr. McCloskey, are admitted with the exception of the excerpt from P210. The reason for denying your request is that we do not consider it relevant to this witness, it not having been put to the witness. Of course, you are not precluded from later on making use of the same document with other witnesses, and then we will decide whether it will be admitted or not. All right. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, what I would like to state that this document, P3852, has no date, and I just wanted to have it in the record. And furthermore, this is a 14-pages long document. The only portion that was shown to the witness was one page with this list, and I don't know whether we should admit the whole document or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A ruling has been made. I can continue to comment on it, but I'm reluctant to since a ruling has been made. If you would like me to, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need any discussion on this. You've put your point on the record, and we know exactly what our role and our function is. So, next witness. Correct me if I am wrong, we are talking of Slavisa Simic, aren't we? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. Can I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- ask for guidance when the next break is going to be. I think I lost some trace of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I have been discussing with our Court officer, and I suggested an hour and a half from when we started, and that means an hour and a half from half past 4.00. Okay, it's 6.00, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break at quarter to, quarter to 6.00, of twenty minutes. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You have been summoned as a witness by the Defence team for accused Borovcanin. Before you start your testimony, you are required to make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable now. Mr. Lazarevic will be asking you some questions. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. I doubt if we will be able to finish today, but we'll try. We'll try. I mean, there is a possibility if he keeps his questions short and to the point. I left the microphone open on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour puts me in a very difficult situation right now, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, I'll introduce myself to you, although naturally, we have already met on a couple of occasions. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic, and together with my colleagues, I am defending Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin before this Tribunal. As in the case of all other witnesses that I examine, whether it's examination-in-chief or cross-examination, I would just like to draw your attention to -- to the following. Since we speak the same language, please wait for me to the complete my question, and only then answer the question so that we can avoid overlapping, which would cause problems for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, can you give us your full name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. McCloskey, we were trying to see how we could economise on time, and our suggestion is -- suggestion to Mr. Lazarevic is with reference to the first two paragraphs of the summary that you are in possession of and that we are in possession of, the summary of this witness, the 65 ter summary, that in relation to the first two paragraphs he can lead, provided there is no objection from the Prosecution, and that he can then put all the questions he wishes in relation to the rest, which appears to be, at least on the face of it, the more substantial part of his would-be testimony. I am sure we'll gain at least 30 minutes. You can easily say, no, I oppose, and we'll proceed as normal, and we'll have lost two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You won't object. All right. So you can lead Mr. Lazarevic. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did, and I will go through this question in a leading fashion so we'll finish with this in the most efficient way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you concentrate on the second half of that summary, which is what is more interesting and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Maybe just one -- one more thing. I mean, in our proofing notes, there are reference to many other events, which I believe I'll have to go through with this witness. It's not just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not restricting you in any way. We are just trying to simplify --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. So just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Having him saying that, I don't see we're going to gain any time because as we saw from the last witness, he led him through the first two paragraphs anyway. If it's the fast leading, I have no problem, but if he's going to still ask stuff about these first two paragraphs, it defeats the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My idea was if you do not have the intention of adding anything to what is contained in the first two paragraphs, then you can lead. If you want to add more, then obviously, I mean, let's proceed in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are some things that I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- like to add, and I will do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed in the normal way. Let's proceed in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise, Mr. Simic. I put a question to you. Could you for the sake of the transcript tell me your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Slavisa Simic. I was born on the 7th of December, 1971, in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I have completed my primary and secondary school, education in Bratunac. Later, I studied in Republika Srpska. I have qualified as an economic technician, and I currently work in the police station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak up a little and to speak more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are -- I am at least not receiving interpretation. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The interpreter has told us that you should speak up a little and perhaps a little more clearly. That's what it says, so if possible, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the warning to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Okay, but I couldn't understand what you were saying in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, sir. You told us about where you were worked. Could you tell us where you lived at the time that the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, I was living in Bratunac together with my family in my father's home in the settlement of Rakovac, which is in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If my colleague McCloskey allows me to do so, I will put a few leading questions to you so that we can get through this a little more quickly. At the beginning of the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina around April, you were mobilized into the Territorial Defence in Bratunac municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And afterwards -- after that, you joined the intervention platoon that was called the Red Berets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's quite enough. These are questions that you can answer by just saying yes or no. And while you were a member of the Red Beret platoon, Bosko Meskovic [phoen] was your commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And that unit at the time was under the command of the 1st Bircani brigade was under, or rather, the 5th battalion in Bratunac, and subsequently it was under the command of the Bratunac brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's the information I have too. At the beginning of the conflict, we were part of the Bircani unit, which had its headquarters in Bratunac, and later on towards the end of 1992 we came under the military post Bratunac. 8042 [as interpreted] was the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise. The number in the transcript doesn't correspond to what you said. Could you repeat the number of the military post in Bratunac, or rather, of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 7042. That's the number that the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you at one point join the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That happened on the 8th of March, 1993. I joined the reserve police force of the Bratunac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now, I would like to ask you the following: From the time that you joined the reserve police force -- well, after that, did you receive training of any kind, policemen, where and when if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That year in July, I would say in 1993, I went to Jahorina for training. There was a police course that lasted for three months that was held there. Upon completing that training course, we returned to the police station where we had another three months of internship, and then we received a decision on employment, pursuant to which I was granted the profession of policemen in the Bratunac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you also receive an official ID card, a badge, and so on and so forth on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down and please don't overlap, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Simic. This was my mistake. I moved on too rapidly after your answer. Could you just repeat your answer, as it hasn't been recorded in the transcript. I asked you whether you received a badge, a police ID, and all other such items that policemen who are employed in police stations have?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me something about the event that resulted in you leaving your post for a lengthy period of time? When did that happen and why? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of December, 1993, I had a car accident on the way from my home to the Bratunac police station. I was, in fact, a pedestrian, and there was an accident. There was a passenger vehicle that was involved. And as a result of the accident, my lower limbs were seriously injured, and there were also injuries to my head and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, we won't go into all the details, but how much time did you spend in hospital, and how much time was spent on rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: It took me over a year and a half to recover. So in July 1995, I returned to my post for policemen in the Bratunac police station, and that's when my sick leave came to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Given your answer, your sick leave was terminated. That's what you said. Had you fully recovered or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the injuries are concerned, they were partially treated successfully. There were two treatments, physiotherapy treatments, so I could to an extent walk normally. But to this very day, I have a first-degree invalidity, and that will remain with me until the end of my days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have first-degree disability. Now, do you know Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin? Can you tell me that now, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin. He was my commander in the Bratunac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you known Mr. Borovcanin? Did you know him before you joined the Bratunac police, or was it on that occasion that you met him? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I first saw him on the 8th of March, 1993, when I first joined the police station. He received me in his office for a short interview, and that's when I remained working at the police station after this first encounter with Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: From the day when you joined the police station until the moment you were injured, Mr. Borovcanin was your commander, wasn't he? Was he transferred to another post during that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of the police station. He did not perform any other duties. He did not hold any other posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And while you worked there, what was the relationship between Mr. Borovcanin with yourself and the other members of the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: My relationship with the commander as well as the relationship of my other colleagues with the commander was very professional, very fair while on duty and off duty because we are talking about a professional -- a good commander who did his job well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the year 1995. You have already told us that at the beginning of July of that year, you returned to work. Given your health condition at the time, what tasks and duties were you assigned to perform at the Bratunac police station when you returned from your sick leave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: It was a duty officer at the police; in other words, I performed the duties of the desk officer or the duty officer at the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when we are talking about the duties of -- of the duty officer, are we talking about regular police duties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What type of uniform did you wear while performing those tasks and duties in the course of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I had a camouflage police uniform like all the other policemen who were attached to that police station at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "camouflage police uniform," would you be able to tell us what its basic colour was? It was a camouflage uniform, but of predominantly what colour? Was it green, blue, or some other colour? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: It was a kind of navy blue, dark blue colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When performing your tasks and duties as a duty officer, did you carry weapons? If you did, what kind?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had my own personal weapon that had been issued to me. It was a police pistol, and I also had other things that police officers normally carry, and I also had a semi-automatic rifle that had been issued to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the time in July 1995, who was the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: In 1995, the chief of the public security station was Miodrag Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And who was the commander of that same station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: The commander was Slavoljub Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior? Who did you report to at the Bratunac public security station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: It was my commander whom I've already named, Slavoljub Mladjenovic. I reported to him. He was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I am going to slow down for the record. Did the public security station in Bratunac belong to a security services centre? If that was the case, could you please name the centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Bratunac public security station at the time belonged to the security services centre or CJB in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The English translation is "public security centre." Here it says "security service centre." This is how we refer to it, just to make a sure that we have clear transcript on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay now. Mr. Simic, could you please tell me who was the chief of the CJB in Zvornik in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: At the time, the chief of that centre was Dragomir Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just a few more questions about your tasks at the station. The first one is this: Did you have a police rank in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I just had a functional marking of a policeman at the time. I did not hold any ranks at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In addition to being a duty officer at the station, were you deployed to perform any other tasks or duties within your station? I'm again talking about July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: All I did at the time was duty service. I was a so-called duty policeman. Later on in a subsequent period, I became a member of the crime prevention police in Bratunac, and I am affiliated with the same department to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now just one more question with this regard. Could you please tell me, were you a member in July, again, of the so-called special police units or PJPs?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... called "special police units here" in [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We always have the same problem with special police or PJPs. My question to you is: Were you a member of a PJP?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of a PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: My health condition, the fact that I had been injured, the disability that I still have. My physical abilities are limited. I have a physical handicap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know - and we are still talking about the year 1995 - do you know that there were police staffs, that they existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe that one such staff of the police forces was headquartered at the CJB in Zvornik, and on the eve of the events in Srebrenica it was transferred to the police station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for clarification, it's not really clear to me what this is, this police staff. It wasn't from the other witness, either. So before we continue referring to it, could we just get what it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. My colleague could have cleared this up with the previous witness or with our expert, but I will try to do it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, what is a police staff, to your best knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: It's a staff composed of the leading men in the centre, the commanding officers of the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was this staff in a position to exert command over the police forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm not really clear what you're asking me. In any case, those were superior officers, the commanding officers of the-then police forces. I suppose that they were in a position to issue tasks to subordinated policemen. That, at least, is my view of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. To the best of your recollection, you said that that staff had been moved to Bratunac. If you can remember, for how long did it continue operating from Bratunac? If you can remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer this question. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, what staff? I mean, there's an objection for, you know, foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the witness said that there was a police staff. I apologise. I don't want to speak about this in front of the witness. He has his earphones, but he can remove them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, but are you referring to the same thing that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the same police [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- that existed in Zvornik, moved eventually to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we just get who? Because all we've got is that a commanding officer unit came down and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you help us, Mr. Simic? You followed the discussion, and in a way it was better to have you follow the discussion. There is obviously a query from the Prosecution as to what staff we're talking about. Can you enlighten us on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already said that the chief of the centre at the time was Dragomir Vasic. He was one, and then his deputy, his assistants subordinated to him, I believe that his deputy at the time was Mane Djuric, those are officers who were above my level at that time. They were the ones who made up this police forces staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's time for the break. We will have a break of 20 minutes. Thank you. --- Break taken at 5.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission I would like to clarify this issue which was raised by my learned colleague about police staff with two documents. I didn't show them earlier to this witness. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- they are not on our list, so just to make sure that we are talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Simic. Since my learned friend wanted to have some issues clarified with regard to the police staffs, I would like us to look at two documents which you have not seen before, but we will call them up in e-court, and you will see what they are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce 4D244.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, look at the document. You will see that this is a report from a meeting of the staff of the police forces of centre, and we can see that this is the public security centre in Zvornik, and we can also see the date when this dispatch was sent. It was done on the 21st of March, 1995. I would like to draw your attention to the first paragraph. The document was sent to the MUP of the Republika Srpska in Bijeljina, to the office of the minister, as well, and it says here: "Acting on your order, a meeting of the police forces staff of the Zvornik public security centre was held on 21st March, 1995." And I believe that we do not need to read any further. My question to you is this, sir: Does it transpire from this document that there was indeed a police staff, and does the document say when they held their meeting? Can you see when this was --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I was waiting for the end of your question. I can see the date, 21st of March, 1995, but I've not seen this document before. And the text that you have just read out reflects what I read in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce P66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we see who wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. [Interpretation] I apologise. Before we do that, can we please move to the following page of the document that we have on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you see who the signatory of the document is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, do. Dragomir Vasic, the centre chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And now can we go to the next document, P66.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, we see that this is a document issued by the public security centre in Zvornik and sent to the same addressees: The MUP RS Bijeljina, the office of the minister, the Bijeljina MUP police headquarters. The date is 1 August 1995. Let's look at the first paragraph of this dispatch. It says: "Acting in accordance with your dispatch, we have held a session of the War Staff of the centre, which has been working continuously since your order of 21 March 1995." If you recall the previous document, would that be the date that is referred to within this document, the date since which the staff has been in operation continuously?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the next page of the document so that we can see the signature. Can we see that the chief of the centre, Mr. Vasic, signed it, too?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And there is one more document I would like to have a look at -- I would like us to have a look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D333.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at this document, then. I know that you haven't seen it before, but I believe that we'll be able to clarify what is at stake here very easily. It's another dispatch sent on the 9th of July, 1995, sent to the MUP of Republika Srpska Pale, the office of the minister, and to the RS MUP Bijeljina, the police command staff. I am not interested in the contents of the document itself, but I would like us to have a look at the signature, and the date is obviously the 9th of July, 1995. Could we have a look at the bottom of the document? And in the lower part of the document, we can see that it says "Staff commander, Dragomir Vasic."

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But given what we have just seen -- given the documents we have just seen, is this the body that is at stake in the public security centre in Zvornik? Is this the staff that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have said, this is the first time I've seen this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But have you heard people referring to the staff, the police in the Zvornik centre and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I think we have dwelt on this subject for long enough. I apologise for going off on a tangent, but I wanted to clarify certain matters here. Mr. Simic, when did you hear that the Republika Srpska army had entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was on the 11th of July I had received some information about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I won't insist on all the details, but if you can remember, do tell me who you heard this from or how you heard this.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard stories according to which people were assembling in Srebrenica. That was information I received. I was working on that day. I didn't have any concrete information about that, but there were these stories and rumors and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And let me now ask you the following: I would like to move on to the events and to the period of the 10th to the 15th of July, 1995. My introductory question is as follows: In the Bratunac public security station, were records kept of the daily activities so that staff members, records about where they were, whether they were in the police station or outside the police station? Do you remember anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, records were kept. Such records were kept. This had to do with the duties of the staff. There was a working list, and on the basis you draw up a schedule for the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to have a look at 4D620, page 28 in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It should come up on the screen in front of you in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down a little bit, please? No, that's too far. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, now that you have this document before you, are these the records that we were just discussing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see my name here, under number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the first column, we have a number. It says number 21. Second column, position or function; that's empty for you and for all others -- all the others in the list. You have your name and your father's name, which is the middle letter, and then it says service or duty or changes with respect to the last man -- the previous man. The that column is empty too. In the following column, we can see the date, the kind of service, the changes and the number of working hours. So these are the categories that we can see in this list. Now, let's have a look at numbers 1 and 2 in the last column. Does this have to do with dates?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise. In the transcript on the screen I just have this information, but perhaps we could scroll down a bit -- no, that's fine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that's good now. We have numbers 1 and 2 above, 3, 4, 5 -- up to 15. Tell me, do these numbers have to do with the dates of the month?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The days of the month?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we could just scroll up a bit so we can see the top left-hand corner on the page. Which month and year are mentioned here -- are noted down here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's have a look at the first two entries for July 1995. For the 1st and -- 2nd of July in your case, in your case we can see the letters "S" in the boxes. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: It means free on the 1st and 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Had you started working in the police station in Bratunac in the public security station before this initial date, which here is the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't. As I have already said, I started working at the beginning of July, during this period, and here it says that it was on the 3rd, that that was the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that in fact was the first day that you worked upon returning from sick leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, now let's have a look at the following entry, the entry for the 10th of July, and here it says D06 to 14. Tell me, what does "D" mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is an initial for duty service, for the staff member who is to be on duty on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Lower down, it says 8. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: That's a -- those are the working hours, eight hours they are on duty, and that's -- in the previous column, you can see that it's from 6 to 1400 hours: 6 to 1400.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the 11th of July, 1995, the next entry. It says from 6 to 18. Below, it says 12; is that correct? That means that you worked 12 hours on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And here's a general question with regard to this: Did you always stay in the station for the periods of time referred to here, or did you sometimes come earlier, go back later? Did you stay on longer? Can you give us a general picture of how things worked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. As an authorised official, it was my duty to arrive at least half an hour before my duty started, and sometimes I would stay on after work or after my working hours were over. It depended on the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. During that period from the 10th of July onwards, did you ever have the opportunity of meeting Mr. Borovcanin at any point in time? And if so, when was the first time that you met him during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet Borovcanin. It was on the 11th between 12.00 and 1.00. He entered the police station. I was on duty at the time. I saw him entering the police station. I approached him. Since I hadn't seen him for a long time, we just greeted each other, and he went up to the chief's office. That was on the 11th. He took the stairs to go up to the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from greeting each other, did you talk about anything else? Was there conversation of any kind that you would like to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very brief. We greeted each other. I hadn't seen him for a long time. He asked me about my health, my recovery. It was very brief. I saw that he was in a hurry to get to the chief's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. After that meeting, did you see Mr. Borovcanin again on that very same day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's dwell a while, briefly, on that date, the 11th of July, 1995. Tell me, did the Bratunac police station, the SJB, use its staff members to fill up the membership, the staff ranks, of the Zvornik special police brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I just want to intervene for the sake of the transcript. We are talking about the PJP units, since we -- I'll just say PJP, nothing else, so that everyone can follow the record in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you now answer the question, if you remember it, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our police station did allocate staff members to those PJP units, the special police units if there's a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the 11th of July, did you see any PJP members who were members of the SJB, the public security station? If so, which company were they from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to see gatherings on the 11th, a gathering of members of the 1st company. This was an hour or two before the end of my working hours. They came to the station. They were preparing to go somewhere. It wasn't clear to me why they had gathered there, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. To have a clear transcript, we're talking about members of the Bratunac SJB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were members of our Bratunac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We know how long you worked on the 11th of July. Did anything in particular happen that you can remember on that day, apart from what you have already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, my shift ended at 1800 hours on that day. I then went home. The PJP members stayed on in the station after I had left. On that day I could go home to rest, but there is nothing particular that I can remember apart from that. I don't know if you have anything in particular in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If there is nothing in particular you can remember or what happened, what you've said is quite sufficient. Very well. Let's now talk about the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have another look at 4D620, page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, you'll see it on the screen. Can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Here we can see that you were in the police station from 6.00 in the morning until 6.00 in the evening. Is that the period that you spent in the station as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the period that I spent in the police station. I was on duty again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you leave the police station, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't, because when you're on duty, your work has to do with what takes place within the premises of the police station itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A few more questions about this day. Do you know anything about the establishment of the police station in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: What I could emphasize is that on the 12th, our 2nd company, or rather, policemen from the Bratunac police station who were members of the 2nd company went to Srebrenica on that day in order to establish that police station. That's what I knew at the time with regard to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, who was in command of the PJP 2nd company?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Slavoljub Mladjenovic was in command of the 2nd company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Is this the individual who took or escorted the 2nd company to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the person in question. They left on that day. They went to Srebrenica in order to establish the police stations. A significant number of policemen from the Bratunac police station went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. There is just one other document I would like to have a look at. You haven't had the opportunity of seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3109.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Look at the document, please. If you need time to familiarise with its contents, please take time, and then I will put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do need some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Maybe we can scroll down for you -- for your benefit to see the whole text. This is a dispatch which was sent on the 12th of July, 1995. As we can see, it was sent from the public security centre in Zvornik to the MUP of Republika Srpska, to the police headquarters in Bijeljina, to the office of the minister in Pale, and to the public security department. And if we look at the first paragraph of the dispatch, you will see that it says that Petko Pavlovic, acting chief of the Srebrenica SJB, was appointed, he was born in 1957 in Ratkovica and so on and so forth, and the signatory of the document is chief of the centre Dragomir Vasic. It also says here the appointment of commander of the Srebrenica PS and the transfer of 15 soldiers and police are underway, of which you will be informed in due course. Now that we have seen this document, and when we have seen the date, will that tally with your recollection that that was the day when the police station was established in Srebrenica? I'm talking about a public security station in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was also the date when the 2nd company was sent to Srebrenica. As I've already told you, on the 12th of July, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness -- I'll rephrase the question, but the witness already said that he noticed that they left on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What do you remember about the departure of the 2nd company of the PJP to Srebrenica? What date was that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: The 2nd company of the PJP left for Srebrenica on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now let me ask you: To arrive in Srebrenica, which route did the 2nd company have to take? Which places did they have to pass?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, they had to travel along the Bratunac-Zuti Most-Potocari-Srebrenica road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We are still talking about the 12th of July, 1995. Did you stay at work until the end of the shift as it is indicated in the list?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go next once your shift ended?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: When my shift ended, as usually, I went home. Maybe you want me to tell you where my house was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: From the police station, my house; i.e., my father's house where I resided, is at two to two and five -- and-a-half-kilometre distance from that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next date, which is the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the Court please produce again 4D620, page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And let's look at the entry for the 13th of July. It says here that your shift started at 1800 hours, and your shift lasted until 2400 hours, and then you continued on the 14th from 000 to 0600; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So these are practically two 6-hour shifts, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The total shift lasted 12 hours and lasted from 13th to the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Does this reflect the time when you arrived at the police station on the 13th of July, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I always tried to come to work half an hour or even one hour before, but the time indicated here is the beginning of my shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few more things. When you arrived at the station, did you learn at that time about the death of a colleague of yours? If you did, could you please tell us who that was and what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I learned that my colleague, a policemen, Zeljko Ninkovic, was killed, and that's why I came to work a little earlier. I was curious about the details of his death, what happened and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Borovcanin on that day? If you did, what were the circumstances of your encounter, if there was one?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: On that day, I did see Mr. Borovcanin at the police station in the corridor in front of the duty officers' room. I was in the middle of a conversation with my colleague, and we were discussing the circumstances of our late colleague's death. I noticed that Mr. Borovcanin had arrived at the Bratunac police station about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us in your own words how the things continued? What happened? Did you talk to him? What about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I noticed that Mr. Borovcanin was agitated, angry. I'd never seen him with such an expression on his face before. He entered the police station. He wanted to make a telephone call, and he went upstairs to the chief's room or to the signals' men room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you alone, or rather, you have already said that you were in the middle of a conversation with another colleague and that you were talking about the death of your colleague. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: It was Dragan Neskovic, a colleague of mine. When I entered the police station in Bratunac, he was coming down the stairs at that moment. Since I knew that he [Realtime transcript read in error, "I"] was the head of maintenance and that he was also in -- responsible for the arrangements about -- that had to do with the death, I wanted to the learn about the funeral of the -- our late colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction in the transcript. Page 78, line 22, it says that [In English] "He was the head of maintenance." [Interpretation] It says: "I was the head of maintenance," and it should read "He was the head of maintenance."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I believe that this is clear now. When you saw Mr. Borovcanin, did you talk to him, or what you have just told us, is this all you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: As I've told you, all he said was that he needed to make an urgent telephone call, and he went upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to learn whether Mr. Borovcanin did make that telephone call? Who did he call? Do you know anything about the contents of that conversation that might have taken place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I could not hear that. I was not in a position to know that because I remained on the ground floor, and then I went to the duty officers' room to take my shift, and the two rooms are physically separate from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you a very general question. Given Mr. Borovcanin's line of command and his position in the special brigade of the police, did he have any command role with regard to the public security station that you belonged to? Was he in a position to issue any orders to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, I could not receive any orders. My superior officer was the commander of the police station in Bratunac. That's who I received orders from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now, talking about the night between the 13th and the 14th of July when you were on duty at the police station, did you learn at any point in time that during that night a large number of Muslim detainees had been brought to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard stories to that effect. I heard rumors to that effect. The story had it that the Muslims were transported by buses from Potocari in the direction of the federation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's relating rumours. That doesn't do us any good, which is what he's just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let him finish, Mr. McCloskey. Let him finish because there are rumours and rumours. Go ahead, Mr. Simic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I already said it, those were rumours. While I was working at the police station on the day, I could not see any transports. I could only listen to what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who you heard the story from, if you can remember, if you can?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember exactly who I heard this from. I can only speculate if you wish me to do that. I wouldn't be able to give you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, we don't want to speculate, sir. In very general terms, what was the number of the policemen in the police station in Bratunac on the 13th of July? Were there enough policemen? Were there people who were on leave? Were there enough men at the disposal for work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's compound, and, you know, there's never enough of anything, so I think that's part of a compound question that is -- doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is definitely a compound question. If you could simplify it, and we've got five minutes left, Mr. Lazarevic. And I'm working with a handicap because my LiveNote has gone kaput.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll do that -- I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of your recollection, how many policemen were there at the police station in Bratunac on the 13th of July? I'm not insisting on the exact and correct number. Give me just the best approximation you can.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Very few policemen were on duty, not more than one patrol. There was also me as the policemen on duty and the deputy commander of the station. As I've already told you, most of them had left on the 12th. They went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Slight clarification. You're speaking about people at the police station. He's talking about people on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I asked you about the physical presence at the public security station in Bratunac. The body count in Bratunac, is that what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other policemen that were available in addition to the ones that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: I've just said that there was just one patrol, one group on control. But again, we're talking about two or three men, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well [Realtime translation read in error, "many"]. Was that enough to maintain, or rather, to perform basic policing that included maintenance of public law and order in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA SIMIC
utterances.text: That was not enough. The number was insufficient. It would take a second patrol to fulfill the task, but the circumstances were rather unusual, and we only had two or three men in that one patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make a correction in the transcript. Page 82, line 3, my question apparently starts with "very many," although my question actually started with "very well." I would like this correction to be made in the transcript to set the record clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I am not starting on another topic. Maybe it's time to adjourn for tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can stop here. Mr. Simic, we are going to stop here for today. We'll continue tomorrow, and hopefully we'll finish with you tomorrow. Before you leave this courtroom, I need to inform you that according to our rules, between now and when you resume your testimony tomorrow, you are not to communicate with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are adjourned until tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of October, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
